bib.title: Spider: A Large-Scale Human-Labeled Dataset for Complex and Cross-Domain Semantic Parsing and Text-to-SQL Task

question: Can a large, human-labeled text-to-SQL dataset with complex SQL and many multi-table databases, split so test databases are unseen, measure real generalisation in semantic parsing?
hypothesis: Existing models score high on prior datasets by memorising query templates; on unseen databases and complex SQL they will fail.
contributions: Spider: 10,181 questions, 5,693 SQL, 200 multi-table databases, 138 domains
A cross-domain task where train and test share no databases or SQL
Evaluation metrics: component matching, exact matching, execution accuracy, hardness levels
Baseline results of six models showing low accuracy

method.summary: Eleven CS students wrote and reviewed questions and SQL over 200 databases in five stages. Existing neural parsers were adapted (schema as concatenated column list, vocabulary mask) and trained on Spider under example and database splits.

datasets.name: Spider
datasets.size: 10,181 questions; 5,693 SQL; 200 DBs (plus 752 queries and 1659 questions from Restaurants, GeoQuery, Scholar, Academic, IMDB, Yelp in final training set)
datasets.split: Example split: 7862 train / 1831 dev / 2147 test. Database split: 206 DBs into 130 train / 36 dev / 40 test
datasets.source: ~70 DBs from courses/tutorials/csv/textbooks; ~40 from DatabaseAnswers converted to SQLite and populated with filldb.info; 90 built from WikiSQL tables (~500 tables, ~90 domains). Licence not stated
datasets.preprocessing: Abbreviated column names (stu_id) manually expanded to words; schemas corrected; values not evaluated

models.name: Seq2Seq+Copying
models.architecture: attention-based copying, like Jia and Liang 2016

models.name: Iyer et al. (2017)
models.architecture: attention seq2seq; user interaction not used

models.name: SQLNet
models.architecture: sketch-based slot filling with column attention; SELECT/WHERE modules extended to other components

models.name: TypeSQL
models.architecture: SQLNet plus type info from DB content; modules extended

other.input_adaptation: concatenate all columns of the question's database into a 'big' column list; restrict column choices to that database
other.schema_handling_seq2seq: vocabulary mask limiting decoding to SQL keywords plus table and column names of current DB

metrics.name: Component Matching
metrics.definition: F1 of exact set match per component (SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY, ORDER BY, KEYWORDS), each decomposed as bag of sub-components

metrics.name: Exact Matching
metrics.definition: predicted query correct only if all components match as sets

metrics.name: Execution Accuracy
metrics.definition: same result on the SQLite database; paper gave no results (deferred to website)

metrics.name: Hardness
metrics.definition: easy/medium/hard/extra hard by number of SQL components, selections, conditions

eval.protocol: Single reported number per cell; no seeds, variance or significance; values not predicted or evaluated

evidence.quote: Database split where 206 databases are randomly split into 130 train, 36 dev, and 40 test

results.claim: Best model (TypeSQL) reaches only 9.7% exact-match accuracy on the database split.
results.setup: Spider test, database split (40 test DBs), TypeSQL with question type info from DB content, all hardness levels
results.quote: The best model achieves only 9.7% exact matching accuracy in the database split setting.
results.note: Abstract says 'best model achieves only 9.7% exact matching accuracy on a database split setting'

results.claim: Same TypeSQL model gets 34.3% under the example split, 3.5x the database-split score.
results.setup: Spider test, example split (7862/1831/2147), TypeSQL, all hardness
results.table: Table 2, row TypeSQL (Example Split), column All

results.claim: Vanilla Seq2Seq drops from 11.2% to 5.4% moving from example split to database split.
results.table: Table 2, row Seq2Seq (Database Split), column All

results.claim: Under database split TypeSQL scores 29.6% on easy but 0.3% on extra hard.
results.setup: Spider test, database split, TypeSQL, extra hard vs easy
results.table: Table 2, row TypeSQL (Database Split), column Extra Hard

results.claim: Under database split, SQLNet is 8.3% overall, with WHERE F1 18.0% and SELECT F1 24.0%; column selection is poor for all models.
results.table: Table 2, row SQLNet (Database Split), column All; Table 3 SQLNet Database Split

results.claim: Accuracy falls as the number of foreign keys in the database grows (schema complexity).
results.setup: Fig 4, exact match vs foreign-key count
results.note: Only a qualitative statement in text; numbers only in the figure

results.claim: Spider has 10,181 questions, 5,693 unique SQL queries, 200 databases, 138 domains, annotated by 11 students.
results.setup: Full corpus before adding 752 queries/1659 questions from six existing datasets
results.quote: It consists of 10,181 questions and 5,693 unique complex SQL queries on 200 databases with multiple tables covering 138 different domains.
results.note: Split section says 206 databases (200 + six existing datasets)

results.claim: Building the corpus took about 1,000 man-hours of annotation.
results.setup: Five-stage process (Fig 2): DB creation 150, annotation 500, SQL review 150, question review 150, final review 150

results.claim: Average database has 28 columns and 9 foreign keys; average question length about 13, SQL length about 21.
results.quote: On average, each database in Spider has 28 columns and 9 foreign keys.

results.claim: Spider averages 5.1 tables per DB versus 1 for WikiSQL, with 1335 ORDER BY, 1491 GROUP BY, 844 nested and 388 HAVING queries.
results.table: Table 1, row Spider, column # Table / DB

results.claim: WikiSQL has about 80,654 questions over 26,521 single-table databases and no JOIN/GROUP BY/ORDER BY.
results.note: Text elsewhere says about 90,000 questions and about 26,000 databases

limits: Training hyperparameters, optimizers, epochs and seeds are not given for any baseline
Execution accuracy defined but results deferred to website (footnote 4)
Condition values are not predicted or evaluated
Questions needing outside knowledge or common sense, and ambiguous questions, are excluded; authors concede ambiguity exists in real interfaces
Column names were manually cleaned, so real abbreviated schemas are not tested
Baselines are 2014-2018 neural parsers; no LLMs, and scores have since been far surpassed
Database counts inconsistent: 200 in abstract, 206 in split (adds six existing datasets)
Foreign-key effect shown only as a plot, no numbers
